seo.title: Stop Your MCP Tool Looking Frozen
seo.hook: A tool that runs for thirty seconds and says nothing looks broken.
seo.description: Two server calls and two client callbacks turn a frozen-looking tool into one that reports itself.

scenes.narration: A tool that runs for thirty seconds and says nothing looks broken.

scenes.headline: The server [speaks up]
scenes.caption: two calls
scenes.premise: A tool that takes thirty seconds is silent by default. These two calls are the only way the user learns anything is happening.
scenes.narration: On the server side there're exactly two calls worth knowing, and they do different jobs. |C t x dot info sends a log line — a human sentence about what's happening right now. ^Searching Wikipedia, for instance. |C t x dot report progress sends a number instead: how far through, out of how much. ^Thirty out of a hundred. |As the work moves on you send more of both, ^writing report, ^and eighty percent. Neither call changes what the tool returns, because they're side channels that travel while the tool is still running — which is exactly why they're useful.

lines.detail: A human sentence about right now.
A number: how far, out of how much.
More of both, as the work moves.

scenes.headline: And letting them [stop it]
scenes.caption: the other half
scenes.premise: Progress tells the user the work is alive. Cancellation lets them end it. A long tool needs both.
scenes.narration: Progress solves half the problem. Here's the other half, and the spec lists it as a core utility alongside progress: cancellation. |If a request can run for thirty seconds, the person watching needs a way to stop it — otherwise your only honest option is making them wait for something they no longer want. ^When the client cancels, your tool's async task is cancelled underneath you, |so the shape that saves you is an ordinary try and finally: ^clean up whatever you opened, then let the cancellation propagate. |Swallowing it is the mistake — ^catch and ignore, and you've built a tool nobody can stop. ^And if the work is genuinely long, minutes rather than seconds, that's what the Tasks extension is for: it hands back a durable handle you poll, instead of holding a request open and hoping.

That builds a tool nobody can stop.
